input: Learn to identify local bird species by call

keyUnknowns.whyItMatters: The number of target species dramatically changes the plan — learning 10 backyard birds is a weekend project, while mastering 100+ regional species requires months of structured study.
The specific geographic region or habitat (e.g. Pacific Northwest forest, UK countryside, Australian suburb) determines which species and sound libraries are relevant.
Whether this is purely self-directed or involves joining a group (birdwatching club, guided walks) changes what resources and social accountability structures to include.
How much time per week the user can commit shapes whether the plan is intensive or slow-burn, and determines milestones.
Knowing what 'done' looks like — casual recognition on a walk vs. passing a formal ID quiz vs. contributing to citizen science — sets the bar for the whole plan.

People learn bird calls very differently: some prefer apps with spaced-repetition quizzes, others favour field trips, recordings, or mnemonics. The preferred style shapes every resource recommendation.
Knowing the user's starting experience level (complete beginner vs. already knows some species by sight) determines how much foundational content to include before diving into audio training.

gold.taskTitle: Learn to identify local bird species by call
gold.taskDescription: The user wants to develop the skill of recognising bird species by listening to their calls and songs in their local area.

questions.title: How many bird species are you aiming to learn?
questions.description: Establish the scope — a small set of common backyard birds, all species in a specific habitat, or a broad regional list — to size the plan appropriately.

questions.title: Which region or habitat will you be listening in?
questions.description: Identify the geographic area or ecosystem (e.g. woodland, coastal, suburban garden) to select the correct species list and sound references.

questions.title: How much time per week can you dedicate to this?
questions.description: Determine the weekly time budget to set a realistic pace, milestone schedule, and session length for practice.

questions.title: What does success look like for you specifically?
questions.description: Clarify the end goal — casual enjoyment on walks, confidently naming every call heard, contributing to a citizen science project, etc. — to define the finish line.

questions.title: Do you prefer app-based drills, field trips, or recordings?
questions.description: Identify the preferred learning style and medium so resources (apps, guided walks, audio libraries, mnemonics) can be matched to how the user retains information best.

questions.title: Will you learn solo or with a group or mentor?
questions.description: Determine whether the user wants to join a birdwatching club, find a local expert, or go it alone, as this shapes accountability and feedback mechanisms.

questions.title: How familiar are you with local birds right now?
questions.description: Gauge the starting experience level — complete beginner, knows birds by sight but not call, or already recognises a few calls — to calibrate where the plan begins.
